title: Processions
hookLine: Holy Week in Seville, Corpus Christi in villages: faith in the streets

lines: A PLATFORM CARRIED BY HIDDEN BEARERS.
cards: Late at night in a narrow street in Seville, during Holy Week. The crowd is packed so tight nobody can turn around. Then a slow drum, and a hush.
Around the corner sways a huge wooden platform, lit by rows of candles, carrying a figure of Christ bent under his cross.
The bearers are hidden underneath, shoulders to the beams, moving in step to a voice calling from outside. In front walk long lines of penitents in robes and tall pointed hoods, holding candles.
A woman on a balcony sings a short, raw song to the figure as it passes.

teach.b: Start with a crowd on a road. As Jesus rides into Jerusalem, people spread cloaks and cut branches, walking ahead and behind him, shouting.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest."
You met that road in your first year, and on Palm Sunday Catholics repeat the walk with branches in hand. A procession is faith that moves. Next, Seville.
In Holy Week its brotherhoods, lay associations of Catholics, carry images of Christ and Mary through the streets. The pointed hoods are penitents' hoods.
Tradition says they hide the face so the penance is offered without anyone knowing who is doing it. The bearers underneath are hidden too.

The whole thing is built so the images are seen and the people aren't. Then a quieter scene. On Corpus Christi, the priest carries the Eucharist in a monstrance, under a canopy, through a parish or village.
In some villages people lay carpets of flower petals and colored sawdust for it to pass over, carpets trampled in minutes.
Church law asks for a public procession on this feast where it can be done, as a public witness of reverence. Last, why walk at all? A church building holds faith still.

teach.h: BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.
teach.b: A procession takes it out the door, past the bakery and the bus stop, and says, without a sermon, that God isn't only indoors, and that the Church is a people on the move, walking somewhere together.

how: Catholics walk in procession with palms on Palm Sunday and, in some places, follow the Eucharist through the streets on Corpus Christi. In Seville and elsewhere in Spain, lay brotherhoods carry images of Christ and Mary through the streets during Holy Week.

games.q: you're a bearer under a Holy Week platform in Seville. the crowd outside can't see you. why is it built that way?
o: so nobody can take credit: the images are seen, the people aren't.
because the bearers are not allowed to watch the procession.
to keep the platform's weight secret.
games.why: the bearers underneath and the hooded penitents in front are hidden alike. the whole procession is arranged so the images are seen, and the people aren't.

practice: If you can, step outside or walk to a window, and notice the street: who passes, what's open, what you hear.
Take a few slow steps in time with your breath, as if in a procession; if you can't move today, let your eyes do the walking.
If you pray, say the Hosanna line quietly or carry someone in your prayer; if you don't, carry a good wish for each person you see.

wordCard.voice: Processions. The Church walking together through the streets with branches, images or the Eucharist: on Palm Sunday, in Holy Week, on Corpus Christi. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek spelling of a Hebrew cry, the shout of the Palm Sunday crowd on the road.

carryVoice: Your line: faith in the streets. A small procession of one still counts. See you tomorrow.
